Sample text:
---
On the first Tuesday of every month, the town of Bellwether auctioned off the things people had left on its buses. Umbrellas went in bundles of five. Telephones went in a cardboard box marked AS IS, which was also how the auctioneer described a wedding dress, a trombone, and a jar containing twenty-seven human teeth.

The teeth went for eleven dollars. The wedding dress took three months.

Mara worked the auction table. Her job was to write down what things sold for, which meant she knew that a good winter coat was worth less in February than in October, and that people would bid against their own spouses for a decent flashlight. She also knew enough not to try on the coats. There was always something in a pocket: a hair clip, a grocery list, a paper napkin with a telephone number. The coat was easy to sell. The napkin was not.

One Tuesday, just before the doors opened, the depot manager set a kitchen chair on her table.

“Number forty-six,” he said.

“How do you leave a chair on a bus?”

“Same way you leave anything. Get off without it.”

It was an ordinary chair, painted yellow except where the paint had worn away under somebody’s elbows. One leg was shorter than the others. Whoever had last sat in it had folded a square of newspaper and tucked it under the leg with a strip of tape.

Mara turned the chair over. The newspaper was dated May 17, thirty-one years earlier. On the exposed square, a supermarket advertised peaches for thirty-nine cents a pound. She tried to remember whether that was cheap even then. Her father would have known. He had kept a running account of what things ought to cost, and long after he stopped going to the shops he would send her out for a loaf of bread with an amount of money that expressed his disapproval.

She put the chair down and opened the doors.

By noon, everything had sold except the chair. Nobody wanted to carry it home. Mara understood. She had taken the bus that morning herself.

“You can put it out back,” the manager said.

Instead, she carried it to the bus stop. It was only two blocks, but there was no good way to hold it. She tried one hand under the seat, then both hands around the back, then an arrangement that left her looking through the slats. At the stop she set it down and sat in it. On the uneven pavement, the short leg turned out to be exactly the right length.

A man with a paper sack stood beside her. After a while he said, “Is that yours?”

“I suppose so.”

“Do you mind?”

She stood. He sat, setting the sack between his shoes. Its bottom was slowly darkening.

“What have you got in there?” she asked.

“A chicken. I was told it was frozen.”

When the bus came, he lifted the sack with both hands. Mara reached for the chair. Then she saw a woman coming down the sidewalk, walking in the careful, irritable way her father used to walk when there was farther to go than he’d counted on. Mara got on the bus without it. From the window she watched the woman put one hand on the back of the chair, test it, and sit.

The chair was still there the following Tuesday. Someone had moved it under the little overhang of the closed tailor’s shop, where it would stay dry if the rain came straight down. Two weeks later there was a cushion on it, the kind people tie to patio furniture. There was no way to tie it to the chair, so someone had tied its strings to each other.

Mara began to notice who used it. Schoolchildren sat in it sideways, with their legs dangling over an arm. A woman who caught the bus at six carried a folded hand towel to put on the seat. Once, after missing her own bus, Mara watched a man in a good suit eat three plums in the chair. He ate them with such concentration that he didn’t notice his bus pull up. Mara hesitated to interrupt, and by then it was too late. He looked up, saw what had happened, and took a fourth plum out of his bag.

In November the chair disappeared. Mara checked behind the tailor’s shop and asked at the depot, where the manager opened the lost-property cupboard without comment. Inside was a single roller skate, a tin of biscuits that rattled too much to contain biscuits, and a wedding dress.

“Another one?” Mara asked.

“Same one.”

She shut the cupboard.

Three days later the chair was back. It had been painted a yellow so bright it looked green next to the brick wall. The cushion was gone. So was the folded newspaper. Whoever had worked on the chair had glued a neat little block of wood to the short leg, so that it rocked on the pavement.

The next time Mara missed her bus, she sat down anyway. She tried keeping both feet on the ground, then crossing her legs. The chair tipped slightly every time she shifted her weight. She took a receipt out of her coat pocket, folded it twice, and slid it under the opposite leg. It worked. Only after she had done it did she look at the receipt. She had bought butter and a birthday card. The card was for her sister, whose birthday had been the previous Thursday. It was still in her bag.

At home, Mara took the card out and wrote, *I bought this on your birthday*. Then she looked at the date on her phone, crossed out *on*, and wrote *near*. The envelope was too wide for the little box outside her building, so she took it with her the next morning to post near the depot.

At the bus stop a boy was sitting in the chair, tying his shoe. His other foot was planted on the folded receipt. Mara waited until he finished before she asked him to lift it. The paper was wet through. She had the birthday card in one hand and the scrap in the other. When the bus came, she gave the boy the card to hold and crouched to fold the receipt one more time.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quiet literary story uses an abandoned chair and its changing caretakers to connect small acts of attention with missed connections.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and gently wry, finding feeling in practical details rather than spelling it out. Mara’s father’s habits, the late birthday card, and the chair’s improvised repairs make time and care feel both imperfect and ongoing. The ending invites the reader to notice how people leave things for one another, and how even an ordinary object can become a place of welcome.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds lost property, modest prices, and everyday objects that carry traces of their owners: the folded newspaper, the receipt, the chair. Its moral emphasis is on care without possession or grand gesture: people adjust the chair, make room for strangers, and pass it along. The moods of loneliness and regret are softened by communal use and practical kindness.

## Evidence line
> The chair was still there the following Tuesday.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the story is coherent and distinctive in how its recurring objects carry its themes, while its understated emotional register is clearly sustained throughout.
